metadata.title: The Status Is A Claim
metadata.series_position: episode 6 — the attestation that refuses to promote itself
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 6, from the last pushed commit on feature/market-sentiment-human-report (8c13b87 == origin head). FRAMEWORK: three questions for any status field — WHAT DID YOU RUN / WHAT DID YOU NOT RUN / DID A GATE SAY NO. Falsifiability beat is B08: nine defects broke during testing, two of them were the gates episode 5 called fixed, and gate 5 had to be fixed twice — so last week's episode shipped a gate that was still wrong. Every figure recounted from the attestation file and the commit itself; see FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: series continuity — episode 5 fixed the gates; this week the gates get to answer back
beats.narration_text: Last episode I gave two gates real failure paths. This week I wrote the attestation — a hundred and twenty-five lines recording what I actually ran. And then the recipe's own lifecycle told me I could not mark it verified. One of the gates I had just fixed was the reason.
beats.new_visual_element: the commit, and the one field it refused to change

shot.show: the commit's seven changed files, and the status field that stayed the same
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards. Left: the commit — 7 files, 177 insertions, the attestation at 125 lines. Right: a single field, status, with RUNNABLE-SAMPLE in it, unchanged. An arrow runs from left to right and stops at a small bar before the right card: the write that did not happen.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions, shown AS A STRUCTURE before any evidence is examined
beats.narration_text: Three questions decide whether a status is a fact or just a claim. One: what did you run — named rows, not a feeling. Two: what did you not run — and is that written down where a reviewer will see it. Three: did a gate say no. Because a recorded refusal has to outrank your own judgment, or it was never a gate.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT DID YOU RUN / WHAT DID YOU NOT RUN / DID A GATE SAY NO
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The third lands in terracotta — it is the question this episode turns on, and the rubric the rest of the reel is scored against.

beats.role_note: the ask, in the composer — what was actually requested of the session
beats.narration_text: The ask was ordinary. Write the attestation in the house format, and then set the status the evidence earns.

shot.show: the composer with the attestation ask

props.command: claude "attest v0.2.0 in the SNICKERDOODLE format — tested, did-not-test, defects — then set status"
props.segment: The ask · write it, then set the status
output: every row names what ran and what was expected
then read the lifecycle before touching status

beats.role_note: QUESTION 1 — what did you run. Verified against the attestation's Tested table.
beats.narration_text: Question one. Seventeen rows, and seven of them are deliberate attempts to break the thing. Eighteen catalogued defects, all eighteen found at the exact location the manifest declares — eight in step three, ten in step four. And a negative check: none of step four's ten leaked into step three's output, so neither step is masking the other.

shot.show: 17 rows / 7 break tests / 18 of 18 defects at declared locators / 0 leaks
shot.visual_intent: Four stat cards in a 2x2 grid, each a bordered box with a large figure and a monospace caption. The 7-break-tests card and the 0-leaks card are terracotta. A citation strip names the attestation file.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 2 — what did you NOT run. The Did-not-test section is the load-bearing half.
beats.narration_text: Question two, and this is the half that makes the format worth anything. Ten entries under Did-not-test. Live execution: never happened, not once. Whether the sentiment score means anything: nobody has checked, the weights came across with no derivation and no author. And wrong-entity rows — a row that is fresh, unique and complete and belongs to a different company. No check here catches it. That class already cost seven hundred and eighty-two purged rows.
beats.new_visual_element: the did-not-test list, with the three that matter named

shot.show: 10 entries, three of them expanded with what each one would cost
shot.visual_intent: A hollow-square checklist of ten unticked boxes down the left — deliberately unticked, that is the point. Three of them expand to the right with a monospace consequence line. The 782-purged-rows figure lands in terracotta on the third.

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — gate 5's four break-test cases, from the attestation
beats.narration_text: Question three. Gate five was break-tested four ways. No live call and no record passes. No live call with a recorded denial passes. A live call with an approval passes. And a live call against a recorded denial must fail — that is the only case that proves the gate reads the decision instead of just counting that one exists.
beats.new_visual_element: the four cases, one of which must fail

shot.show: gate 5's four break-test cases as written in the attestation

props.title: logs/attestations/market-sentiment-analysis-part-1-v0.2.0.md  @ 8c13b87
props.code:
Break test: gate 5 — four cases

  no live call / no record      → PASS
  no live call / decision: deny → PASS
  live call   / decision: deny → FAIL
  live call   / approved        → PASS

  # it reads approved_for_live_action
  # out of the record.
  # existence of a record is not consent.
props.sparkLine: A recorded refusal must not clear the gate

beats.role_note: the verdict the rubric forces — the lifecycle ladder, and where it stops
beats.narration_text: So here is what question three costs. The lifecycle runs draft, specified, runnable-sample, runnable-live, verified. The recipe sits at runnable-sample. Reaching verified means passing through runnable-live, whose test is a live run with a human clearing every gate. No live run exists. Gate five is recorded: deny. Writing verified today would assert a run that never happened and a clearance that was refused.
beats.new_visual_element: the lifecycle ladder with the stop drawn on it

shot.show: DRAFT, SPECIFIED, RUNNABLE-SAMPLE, RUNNABLE-LIVE, VERIFIED — with the stop between the third and fourth
shot.visual_intent: Five chips in a horizontal ladder joined by connectors. The first three are ink; RUNNABLE-SAMPLE gets a filled marker. The connector between RUNNABLE-SAMPLE and RUNNABLE-LIVE is struck with a terracotta bar, and two reason lines sit under it: no live run, and gate 5: deny.

beats.role_note: the commit's own honesty — nine defects broke DURING testing, two of them were the gates themselves
beats.narration_text: The falsifiable part. Nine things broke while I was testing and had to be fixed — and two of them were the gates from last episode. Gate five got fixed twice: first it passed if you did nothing, then it passed on the mere existence of a decision record, so the denial cleared it exactly as an approval would. Which means last week's episode shipped a gate I had already called fixed. The attestation is evidence the testing was real. It is not evidence the thing works.
beats.new_visual_element: the nine defects, with the two self-inflicted ones marked

shot.show: 9 defects found during testing; the two gate defects separated out
shot.visual_intent: A vertical list of nine short monospace rows with small ink ticks. Two rows — gate 4 and gate 5 — sit in a bordered terracotta box pulled out to the right, with 'fixed twice' on the gate 5 row.

beats.role_note: scored against the rubric, then the five steps VERIFIED would actually require
beats.narration_text: Scored. What did I run: seventeen rows, seven of them adversarial. What did I not run: ten entries, written down. Did a gate say no: yes, and the status did not move. What verified would take is already written out in order — implement live mode, build a second fixture set for the HTTP failures, reopen gate five, do a live run with every gate cleared, and write a fresh attestation against whatever version actually ran. Steps one and two are code. Step three is a judgment, and it has already been made once, and it was no.
beats.new_visual_element: the rubric scored, and the five remaining steps

shot.show: three rubric rows answered, then the five numbered steps to VERIFIED
shot.visual_intent: Left column: the three rubric questions, each with a bordered answer chip. Right column: five numbered steps in a connected chain. Step 3 is terracotta and carries 'already answered: no'.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric turned on the viewer's own repo, with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Find something in your project that carries a status — verified, passing, production, ready. Then ask what evidence would have to exist for that word to be true, and whether anything ever said no. If the answer is that nobody checked, the word is a claim.

shot.show: the composer with the handoff prompt and a GOOD/BAD discriminator

props.command: claude "for this status field: list the evidence it asserts, and find anything in the logs that recorded a refusal"
props.segment: Your turn · is the status a claim
output: GOOD: names the evidence each word asserts
BAD: “it is marked ready, so it is ready”
a refusal nobody read is not a gate
